title: Heaven
hook: what no eye has seen (1 Corinthians 2:9)
tomorrow: who's been keeping you company these five years?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: these hands. The Creed ends with the body raised. Which leaves the obvious question: raised into what?

Clouds. A man at a gate with a clipboard. Everyone in white, slightly bored. The cartoon heaven is easy to draw. Paul won't draw it at all. Writing to the church at Corinth, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him." So nobody has seen it. And still, Catholics have talked about it in two ways.
screen: `THE CARTOON HEAVEN.` → `PAUL WON'T DRAW IT.` → `TWO WAYS TO TALK ABOUT IT.`

segments.voice: The first view: heaven is seeing God. Paul again: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Theologians call it the beatific vision, the sight that makes you happy. Its best case: everything you've ever loved, a song, a face, a summer night, was a small reflection of God. Heaven is meeting the original. Nothing left to do, because nothing is missing. The second view: heaven is a world made new. At the end of the Bible, John sees "a new heaven and a new earth," a city with a river, and God wiping away every tear. Its best case: God made a world and called it good. He doesn't throw it away; he finishes it. And yesterday's raised bodies need somewhere to stand. Which one is right? The Church keeps both. The Catechism speaks of seeing God face to face, and also of new heavens and a new earth. One gives you the center, the other gives you the room. Saint Augustine, at the end of The City of God, holds them in one line: there we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise. And both agree with Paul: whatever we picture is smaller than the real thing.
screen: `VIEW ONE: FACE TO FACE.` · `VIEW TWO: A WORLD MADE NEW.` · `THE CHURCH KEEPS BOTH.` · then, large: `WHAT NO EYE HAS SEEN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring back one moment of real joy, the kind you didn't want to end. Hold it, then let it open wider than that moment could, with no clock running and nothing missing. Whatever you find there, Paul says, is still smaller than what no eye has seen.
Heaven. Seeing God face to face, in a world made new: the joy Paul says no eye has seen.
The line to keep: what no eye has seen, and every cartoon of it is too small. See you tomorrow.
